text:
Keep the Pen Moving: The Case for Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years someone declares joined-up handwriting dead. The argument is familiar. Children will spend their adult lives typing, dictating and tapping, so the hours spent in Year 2 and Year 3 learning to loop an "l" into an "e" are a nostalgic hangover from the copperplate era. Some American states dropped cursive from their standards in the 2010s, and several have since quietly brought it back. In England the national curriculum still expects children to join their letters, and every so often a columnist suggests we follow the abolitionists.

We should not. Primary schools should go on teaching joined-up handwriting, and the reasons have little to do with nostalgia or penmanship. The case rests on what handwriting does for a young writer's thinking, on the plain fact that children still write by hand far more than adults assume, and on what happens to the children who never become fluent with a pen.

What joining is for

The weakest version of the pro-cursive argument treats handwriting as a craft worth preserving for its own sake, like calligraphy or dry-stone walling. That argument deserves to lose. If joined writing were only about beauty, it would be a fine after-school club and a poor use of curriculum time.

The stronger argument starts with what joining is for, which is speed and fluency. Lifting the pen after every letter costs time. Each lift is a small break in the motor sequence, and a child printing separate letters has to start each one again: find the spot, place the pen, form the shape, lift. Joining turns a word into one continuous movement, or a few. Once that movement is automatic, a child can write quickly without thinking about the mechanics.

Automaticity is the point. Writing is hard for young children because it asks them to do several things at once. They have to hold an idea in mind, find the words for it, put those words in a sentence, spell them and physically form the letters, all with a working memory that is small to begin with. Researchers in writing development, Virginia Berninger among them, have argued for decades that when letter formation is slow and effortful it takes up attention the child needs for composition. A child concentrating on how to make a "k" is not thinking about what happens next in the story. The usual finding in this research is that handwriting fluency predicts the length and quality of what children compose, and not only how neat it looks.

So the goal is not cursive as such. The goal is handwriting so fluent that it stops being noticed. For most children, joining is the most reliable way to get there, because a joined hand is built to be fast. A curriculum that drops joining does not free children from handwriting. It leaves them with a slower version of it.

Children still write by hand, a lot

The second objection is that none of this matters, because writing will soon be done on screens. That may be true in the long run. It does not describe a primary classroom in 2026, and it barely describes a secondary one.

Children in England do most of their school writing by hand. Exercise books are still the default. Phonics, spelling practice, maths working, science write-ups and the extended writing that teachers assess for end-of-key-stage judgements are overwhelmingly done on paper. Above all, high-stakes exams are still largely handwritten. A sixteen-year-old sitting GCSE English Literature can expect to write for well over an hour under time pressure, by hand. Exam boards have started to experiment with on-screen assessment, and that change may come in time, but it is coming slowly and unevenly. A child entering Reception this year will almost certainly sit some handwritten exams.

In those exams, speed matters. A student who writes slowly writes less, and in essay subjects writing less usually means scoring less. Examiners mark what is on the page, not what the candidate meant to say. The difference between a fluent joined hand and a laborious print can amount to a page or more over a long paper. That is not a question of style. It is a question of fairness, and it falls hardest on the children least likely to have picked up fluent handwriting at home.

The thinking argument

There is a further reason to keep handwriting strong, one that applies whether or not exams move online. The evidence is still developing, and it should be stated carefully, but a growing body of research suggests that writing by hand engages the brain differently from typing.

Neuroscientists at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, for example, have used EEG to compare brain activity in children and young adults while they write by hand and while they type. They report more widespread connectivity, in regions linked to memory and to encoding new information, during handwriting. Studies of letter learning in young children have found that forming letters by hand helps them recognise letters better than selecting them on a keyboard. The well-known finding that students who take notes by hand remember more than those who type them has had a mixed record in replication. Even so, the overall picture is suggestive: making letters with your own hand, in sequence, seems to help with learning and remembering what you write.

None of these studies proves that a joined script beats a fluent unjoined one, and anyone who says so is overselling the research. The honest claim is narrower and still strong enough to matter. Handwriting is worth teaching well, because it seems to support learning in ways keyboards may not, and teaching it well means teaching it to fluency. Joining is how most children reach fluency.

Answering the critics

Opponents of joined-up handwriting make some fair points, and they deserve a straight answer.

The first is that some children find joining hard, especially those with dyspraxia, developmental coordination disorder or other motor difficulties. That is true, and it is a reason for flexibility, not abolition. A sensible policy teaches joining as the default and lets a child who struggles badly use a clear, quick print, or a keyboard where that is the right adjustment. Schools already make adjustments of this kind in plenty of areas. We do not stop teaching reading because some children are dyslexic. We teach reading and support those children properly. The same principle applies here.

The second objection is that time spent on handwriting is time taken from something else, such as coding, or typing, or more reading. But the time involved is modest. A good handwriting programme needs short, frequent practice, often ten or fifteen minutes a few times a week, mostly in the early primary years. And it pays for itself, because every later lesson that involves writing goes better when the writing comes easily. Typing deserves a place in the curriculum too, and the two are not rivals. A child can and should learn both.

The third objection concerns pre-cursive and fully cursive scripts, with their lead-in strokes and the occasional demand that children join every letter from the first day of Reception. Some of these approaches are too rigid, and the critics are right to say so. Forcing a four-year-old to add an entry flick to every letter before they can reliably form the letter itself can confuse more than it helps. But that is an argument about method, not about whether to teach joining at all. The approach in the English curriculum is a reasonable one: learn to form letters correctly first, then begin to join in Year 2, and build towards a fluent, legible, personal joined hand by the end of primary school.

The last objection is the cultural one: adults hardly write by hand any more, so why burden children with it? This mixes up what adults do with what children need. Adults mostly do not do long division by hand either, but we still teach it, because working through it builds understanding of number that a calculator does not. Handwriting is similar. Its value in childhood is partly practical and partly developmental, and both survive the fact that a forty-year-old mostly types.

What we would lose

Consider what would happen if joined-up handwriting were dropped. In most schools handwriting would not vanish. Children would still write every day, in print, and many would teach themselves some sort of joining as they speeded up, because joining is what hands naturally do when they hurry. The children who managed this would be fine. The ones who did not would be left with a slow, effortful hand going into secondary school, where the demands on writing rise sharply.

Experience suggests which children those would be. They are the ones with less practice at home, less adult help, and fewer chances to fill in what school leaves out. Handwriting instruction is one of the more equalising things a primary school does. It is explicit, it can be taught, and it does not rely on cultural capital. Removing it would not free children from an outdated skill. It would turn a skill that school teaches into one that families have to provide.

Joined-up handwriting is not sacred, and it does not need to look beautiful. Children do not need to write in copperplate, and they do not all need to join in the same way. What they need is to write quickly, legibly and without thinking about it, so that their attention can go to what they are trying to say. For most children, a joined hand is still the surest way to get there. Primary schools should keep teaching it, with flexibility for children who need something different, until the day children stop being asked to write by hand. That day is still a long way off.
